chunks: Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Mahbub, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub, from Isa ibn Sabih, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the thief who steals from the top of a wall (al-tarrar), the thief who digs into a wall (al-nabbash), and the thief who steals secretly (al-mukhtalis). He said: 'They are not amputated (hand).' So we assume that something may have been omitted from the report, because we have narrated this exact report from Isa ibn Sabih in what preceded, in the narration of al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Ibn Mahbub from him, who said: 'I asked him about these three, and he said: The tarrar and the nabbash are amputated, and the mukhtalis is not amputated.' And even if this detail had not come down, we would have based it on what we based the last two reports on.

key_terms.الطَّرَّار: Thief who steals from the top of a wall or high place
key_terms.المُخْتَلِس: Thief who steals secretly or stealthily
key_terms.النَّبَّاش: Thief who digs into a wall or floor to steal
key_terms.يُقْطَعُ: He is amputated (referring to the hand)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on hand amputation for different types of thieves in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Al-Istibsar* clarifies the jurisprudential distinction in hand amputation (*qat' al-yad*) by differentiating between thieves who steal from above (*tarrar*) or below (*nabbash*) versus those who steal secretly (*mukhtalis*). Shaykh al-Tusi highlights a potential textual omission but resolves it by citing a more precise narration where the former two are exempt while the latter is subject to amputation, reflecting the Shia emphasis on specific conditions of theft. This distinction underscores the scholarly principle of reconciling apparent contradictions in hadith chains through detailed contextual analysis.
